metadata.exam-title: AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer - Associate
metadata.description: Validates expertise in building, training, tuning, and deploying machine learning models on AWS using SageMaker and related services.

question.title: Feature Engineering at Scale
question.scenario: A retail company has 500 million transaction records and wants to create customer features for a recommendation model. Features include purchase frequency, average basket size, and category preferences calculated over various time windows (7 days, 30 days, 90 days). The feature engineering process must be reproducible and features should be available for both training and real-time inference.
question.question-text: Which approach provides scalable feature engineering with training-serving consistency?

choices.choice: Pandas DataFrames in Jupyter notebooks
Custom Python scripts running on a single EC2 instance
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store with SageMaker Data Wrangler for feature definitions
SQL views in Amazon Redshift only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What challenge arises when features computed for training differ from those served at inference time?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Feature Store with Data Wrangler provides enterprise feature engineering. Data Wrangler enables visual feature definition with 300+ built-in transforms for aggregations and time windows. Feature Store maintains both offline store (S3/Parquet for training) and online store (low-latency for inference), ensuring training-serving consistency. Features are versioned and discoverable. Processing scales with SageMaker Processing or Glue for 500M records. Single EC2 can't handle volume. Notebooks aren't reproducible. SQL views don't serve real-time inference.

ul.li: Feature Store online store provides single-digit millisecond feature retrieval
Data Wrangler export generates SageMaker Processing or Glue jobs for production
Time-travel queries retrieve point-in-time feature values for backtesting
Feature groups organize related features with schema versioning
Streaming ingestion via Kinesis enables real-time feature updates

question.title: Hyperparameter Optimization Strategy
question.scenario: A data science team is training a deep learning model for image classification. Training one model takes 8 hours on ml.p3.2xlarge. The team has identified 6 hyperparameters to tune with continuous and categorical values. They have budget for approximately 50 training jobs. The goal is to find optimal hyperparameters efficiently.
question.question-text: Which hyperparameter tuning strategy maximizes optimization efficiency?

choices.choice: SageMaker Hyperparameter Tuning with Bayesian optimization and early stopping
Manual grid search trying all combinations
Random search with uniform sampling
Train with default hyperparameters only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider optimization strategies that learn from previous trials to focus on promising regions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Hyperparameter Tuning with Bayesian optimization efficiently explores the 6-dimensional parameter space. Bayesian optimization builds a probabilistic model of the objective function, focusing trials on promising regions rather than random sampling. With 50 jobs and 8-hour training time, efficiency is critical. Early stopping terminates poorly-performing jobs quickly, saving compute. Warm start reuses learning from previous tuning jobs. Grid search is infeasible with 6 continuous parameters. Random search doesn't learn from results. Default hyperparameters won't optimize performance.

ul.li: Bayesian optimization uses Gaussian Process regression to model the objective surface
Acquisition function (Expected Improvement) balances exploration and exploitation
Early stopping monitors objective metric and terminates jobs unlikely to improve
Warm start transfers knowledge from previous tuning jobs for related models
Hyperband strategy enables aggressive early stopping for faster convergence

question.title: Model Deployment Pattern Selection
question.scenario: An e-commerce company deploys a recommendation model serving 10,000 requests per second at peak. Traffic varies significantly - 5x difference between peak and off-peak hours. Inference latency must be under 50 milliseconds. The model is 500 MB and requires GPU for efficient inference. Cost optimization is important.
question.question-text: Which deployment configuration meets these requirements?

choices.choice: SageMaker Batch Transform processing requests hourly
Single ml.p3.2xlarge instance running continuously
Lambda with container image for inference
SageMaker Real-time Inference with auto-scaling and Inference Recommender for instance selection

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How should a deployment handle 5x traffic swings while keeping latency low and costs reasonable?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Real-time Inference with auto-scaling optimizes for this workload. Auto-scaling adjusts instance count based on traffic, scaling up for peak 10K TPS and down during off-peak for cost efficiency. Inference Recommender benchmarks the model across instance types to find optimal GPU configuration meeting 50ms latency. Application Auto Scaling uses CloudWatch metrics (InvocationsPerInstance) for scaling decisions. Batch Transform doesn't meet real-time requirements. Lambda has cold start issues and 15-minute timeout limits. Single instance can't handle peak load.

ul.li: Inference Recommender tests ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.p3 instances for price-performance
Auto-scaling target tracking maintains target invocations per instance
Multi-model endpoints share infrastructure across multiple models
Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold start for predictable latency
Model compilation with Neo optimizes inference on specific hardware

question.title: Model Performance Monitoring
question.scenario: A credit scoring model in production shows declining approval rates over the past month. The data science team suspects data drift as economic conditions have changed. They need to detect when input feature distributions shift from training data and when model predictions deviate from expected patterns, with automated alerting.
question.question-text: Which monitoring approach detects these issues?

choices.choice: CloudWatch metrics for endpoint invocation counts only
SageMaker Model Monitor with data quality and model quality monitoring schedules
Manual weekly review of prediction distributions
A/B testing with holdout traffic

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider automated monitoring solutions that detect statistical drift in features and predictions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Model Monitor provides comprehensive drift detection. Data quality monitoring compares incoming feature distributions against training baselines using statistical tests, detecting feature drift. Model quality monitoring tracks prediction distributions and, with ground truth labels, actual model performance metrics. Scheduled monitoring jobs run continuously with configurable thresholds. CloudWatch integration enables alerts when violations occur. Manual review is reactive and slow. Invocation counts don't show drift. A/B testing compares models, not drift.

ul.li: Data quality uses Deequ library for statistical constraint validation
Baseline constraints define expected feature ranges, types, and distributions
Model quality metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, and custom metrics
Model bias monitoring detects discriminatory prediction patterns
Feature attribution drift shows which features contribute to prediction changes

question.title: Data Labeling for Supervised Learning
question.scenario: A company is building an object detection model for warehouse inventory. They have 100,000 images that need bounding box annotations. The labeling team has 5 annotators with varying expertise levels. Quality control is essential as mislabeled data will degrade model performance. Budget is limited for this labeling project.
question.question-text: Which service provides cost-effective labeling with quality control?

choices.choice: Manual labeling by each annotator working independently
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth with automated labeling and annotation consolidation
Outsourcing to a general crowdsourcing platform
Using only synthetic data without real annotations

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What matters most when annotators have varying skill levels and the budget is tight?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Ground Truth provides cost-effective labeling with quality control. Automated labeling uses active learning - as annotators label initial data, Ground Truth trains a model to pre-label remaining images, reducing human effort by up to 70%. Annotation consolidation combines multiple annotator labels using consensus algorithms, improving quality. Built-in workforce management supports private teams with configurable workflows. Quality metrics track annotator accuracy. Manual labeling lacks quality controls. Generic crowdsourcing may lack domain expertise. Synthetic data doesn't replace real annotations.

ul.li: Active learning selects most informative samples for human annotation
Annotation consolidation uses expectation maximization for label consensus
Custom workflows define approval processes and quality thresholds
Ground Truth Plus provides fully managed labeling by AWS experts
Pre-built task templates support bounding boxes, semantic segmentation, and more

question.title: Distributed Training Strategy
question.scenario: A research team is training a 10-billion parameter language model. Training on a single GPU would take 6 months. The model is too large to fit in a single GPU's memory. The team needs to reduce training time to 2 weeks using distributed training across multiple nodes while maintaining training stability.
question.question-text: Which distributed training approach handles this large model efficiently?

choices.choice: SageMaker distributed training with model parallelism and tensor parallelism
Data parallelism with synchronized gradient updates
Training on a single ml.p4d.24xlarge instance
Sequential training on multiple smaller models

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What happens when a model simply cannot fit into one GPU's memory, no matter how large the instance?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker distributed training with model parallelism is required for 10B parameter models. Model parallelism partitions the model across GPUs - different layers on different devices - when the model exceeds single GPU memory. Tensor parallelism splits individual layers across devices for very large layers. SageMaker's library automatically optimizes partition placement and communication. Pipeline parallelism overlaps computation and communication for efficiency. Data parallelism alone can't handle models larger than GPU memory. Single instance lacks sufficient memory. Sequential training doesn't reduce time.

ul.li: Model parallelism uses device placement to split transformer layers across GPUs
Tensor parallelism shards attention heads and feed-forward layers across devices
Pipeline parallelism processes micro-batches in parallel stages
Mixed precision (FP16/BF16) reduces memory and accelerates training
Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing activations

question.title: Multi-Model Endpoint Optimization
question.scenario: A SaaS company provides personalized ML models for 500 customers. Each customer has their own trained model (average 100 MB). Models receive varying traffic - some customers have 1000 requests/day, others have 10. Deploying 500 separate endpoints is cost-prohibitive. Inference latency should be under 200 milliseconds.
question.question-text: Which deployment strategy optimizes cost for many models with variable traffic?

choices.choice: SageMaker Multi-Model Endpoints with dynamic model loading
500 individual SageMaker endpoints with minimum instances
Single model trained on all customer data
Lambda functions with embedded models for each customer

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Is there a way to avoid paying for 500 separate endpoints when most models see very little traffic?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Multi-Model Endpoints (MME) provide cost-effective multi-tenancy. MME hosts all 500 models on shared infrastructure. Models load dynamically when invoked - frequently accessed models stay in memory, infrequently used models load on-demand from S3. This dramatically reduces costs versus 500 endpoints. Memory sizing accommodates active model working set. The 100 MB model size fits well within instance memory. 500 endpoints would cost 500x minimum instance costs. Single model loses personalization. Lambda has cold start latency issues.

ul.li: MME uses LRU caching - popular models stay loaded, others evict when memory full
TargetModel header in inference request specifies which model to invoke
Instance sizing: model_count * model_size / memory_ratio estimates required memory
CloudWatch metrics show model loading latency and cache hit rates
Multi-model with GPU supports GPU inference for multiple models

question.title: Explainability for Model Debugging
question.scenario: A loan approval model is rejecting applications at a higher rate than expected. Regulators require explanations for individual decisions. The team needs to understand which features drive specific predictions and identify potential bias in model decisions across different demographic groups.
question.question-text: Which approach provides prediction explainability and bias detection?

choices.choice: Correlation analysis between features and outcomes
SageMaker Clarify for feature attribution, bias metrics, and model explainability reports
Examining model weights directly
Manual review of rejected applications

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Regulators want per-decision reasoning and group-level fairness evidence. Which capabilities does that require?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Clarify provides comprehensive explainability and bias detection. Clarify uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) for feature attribution, showing which features drive individual predictions - essential for regulatory compliance. Bias metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) detect disparate impact across groups. Pre-training bias analysis identifies bias in training data. Post-training analysis detects model-introduced bias. Reports document findings for auditors. Model weights don't explain predictions. Correlation misses interaction effects. Manual review doesn't scale.

ul.li: SHAP values quantify each feature's contribution to moving prediction from baseline
Clarify supports both tabular and NLP model explanations
Bias metrics include CI (Class Imbalance), DPL (Difference in Positive Proportions)
Partial dependence plots show feature impact across value ranges
Real-time explainability provides per-request feature attributions

question.title: Handling Imbalanced Classification Data
question.scenario: A fraud detection model is trained on transaction data where only 0.1% of transactions are fraudulent. The model achieves 99.9% accuracy but fails to detect actual fraud. The team needs techniques to handle this severe class imbalance and improve fraud detection recall without generating too many false positives.
question.question-text: Which combination of techniques addresses class imbalance effectively?

choices.choice: Use accuracy as the sole evaluation metric
Collect more data until classes are balanced
SMOTE oversampling of minority class, class weights in loss function, and threshold tuning on precision-recall curve
Remove majority class samples to balance dataset

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider sampling techniques combined with algorithm modifications for imbalanced data.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The combination of SMOTE, class weights, and threshold tuning addresses imbalance comprehensively. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) generates synthetic fraud samples by interpolating between existing frauds, increasing minority representation. Class weights in the loss function penalize misclassifying fraud more heavily. Threshold tuning on precision-recall curve finds optimal decision boundary balancing recall (catching fraud) and precision (avoiding false positives). Accuracy misleads with imbalanced data. More data rarely achieves balance. Removing majority loses information.

ul.li: SMOTE creates synthetic samples along lines connecting minority class neighbors
Class weights: weight = total_samples / (n_classes * class_samples)
Precision-Recall AUC better evaluates imbalanced classifiers than ROC AUC
Focal loss down-weights easy examples, focusing training on hard cases
Ensemble methods (balanced random forest) help with severe imbalance

question.title: Algorithm Selection for Regression
question.scenario: A real estate company wants to predict house prices based on features like square footage, location, bedrooms, and age. They have 50,000 historical sales records. The relationship between features and price may be non-linear. Model interpretability is important for explaining predictions to clients. Training should complete within a few hours.
question.question-text: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is most appropriate?

choices.choice: DeepAR for time series forecasting
Image Classification for visual analysis
BlazingText for text classification
XGBoost for gradient-boosted tree regression with feature importance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which family of algorithms naturally handles non-linear tabular data while staying interpretable?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: XGBoost is ideal for this tabular regression task. XGBoost's gradient-boosted trees naturally capture non-linear relationships between features and price. Built-in feature importance scores explain which factors (location, size) most influence predictions - essential for client explanations. SageMaker's XGBoost trains efficiently on 50K records within hours. The algorithm handles mixed feature types without extensive preprocessing. DeepAR is for time series. BlazingText is for text. Image Classification is for images.

ul.li: XGBoost feature importance: gain (improvement), cover (samples), and weight (frequency)
SageMaker XGBoost supports distributed training for larger datasets
Early stopping prevents overfitting by monitoring validation metrics
SHAP values provide more detailed feature attribution than built-in importance
Hyperparameters: max_depth, eta (learning rate), num_round control complexity

question.title: Blue-Green Deployment for ML Models
question.scenario: A production recommendation model serves 1 million daily users. The team is deploying a new model version that was trained on recent data. They need to safely roll out the new model, monitor for performance degradation, and have the ability to quickly rollback if issues arise. The transition should not impact user experience.
question.question-text: Which deployment strategy enables safe model updates?

choices.choice: Deploy new model to separate endpoint and switch DNS
Direct endpoint update replacing the old model
Manual A/B testing with 50/50 split
SageMaker deployment guardrails with canary deployment and automatic rollback

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How do you validate a new model on real traffic without risking all users if something goes wrong?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker deployment guardrails with canary deployment provides safe model updates. Canary deployment routes a small percentage (e.g., 5%) of traffic to the new model initially. CloudWatch alarms monitor latency, errors, and custom metrics. If metrics degrade, automatic rollback reverts to the previous model within seconds. Traffic gradually shifts to new model if metrics remain healthy. This prevents full user impact from model issues. Direct update risks all users. Manual A/B lacks automation. DNS switching is slow for rollback.

ul.li: Canary steps: 5% for 10 minutes, 25% for 10 minutes, 100% if healthy
Auto-rollback triggers on CloudWatch alarm breach for error rate or latency
Linear deployment shifts traffic incrementally (10% every 10 minutes)
All-at-once deployment available for non-critical updates
Shadow testing routes traffic to new model without serving responses

question.title: Cost Optimization for ML Workloads
question.scenario: A data science team runs training jobs that take 4-8 hours each, with 20 experiments per week. They also maintain 5 real-time inference endpoints running 24/7. Current monthly costs are $50,000. Management wants 40% cost reduction without impacting model quality or inference latency.
question.question-text: Which combination of strategies achieves the cost reduction?

choices.choice: Reduce number of training experiments
Spot instances for training, right-sized inference instances with auto-scaling, and SageMaker Savings Plans
Use smaller instance types for all workloads
Move all workloads to on-premises infrastructure

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which workloads can tolerate interruption versus which need guaranteed uptime.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The combination of Spot instances, right-sizing, auto-scaling, and Savings Plans achieves 40%+ reduction. Spot instances provide 60-90% savings for training jobs - checkpointing handles interruptions. Inference Recommender right-sizes endpoints to actual requirements. Auto-scaling reduces instance count during low-traffic periods. SageMaker Savings Plans provide additional 30% savings on committed compute. Reducing experiments impacts innovation. Undersized instances hurt performance. On-premises adds complexity without guaranteed savings.

ul.li: Managed Spot Training automatically checkpoints and resumes interrupted jobs
Inference Recommender benchmarks model across 20+ instance types
Scale-to-zero endpoints start from 0 instances for infrequent workloads
Savings Plans apply to SageMaker Studio notebooks, training, and inference
Multi-model endpoints share infrastructure cost across models

question.title: Time Series Feature Engineering
question.scenario: A utility company wants to forecast electricity demand 24 hours ahead. Historical data includes hourly demand, weather, holidays, and events. Demand shows daily, weekly, and seasonal patterns. The team needs to engineer features that capture temporal patterns, lagged relationships, and external factors for accurate forecasting.
question.question-text: Which feature engineering approach captures temporal patterns effectively?

choices.choice: Simple moving average of demand
Only current hour's weather data
Lag features, rolling statistics, Fourier transforms for seasonality, and calendar features
One-hot encoding of hour only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider multiple feature types that capture different aspects of temporal behavior.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Comprehensive temporal features capture the complex demand patterns. Lag features (demand at t-1, t-24, t-168) capture autocorrelation at different horizons. Rolling statistics (mean, std over 24h, 7d) smooth noise and capture trends. Fourier transforms encode daily/weekly/yearly seasonality as continuous features. Calendar features (hour, day of week, holiday flags) capture cyclical patterns and special events. Weather features with appropriate lags account for temperature's delayed impact. Single features miss pattern complexity.

ul.li: Lag selection: partial autocorrelation function (PACF) identifies significant lags
Fourier features: sin(2*pi*hour/24), cos(2*pi*hour/24) for daily cycle
Rolling windows should match forecast horizon to prevent data leakage
Holiday effects often span multiple days (pre/post holiday patterns)
Weather lags: temperature impacts demand with 1-2 hour delay for HVAC

question.title: Transfer Learning for Computer Vision
question.scenario: A manufacturing company needs to detect defects in products using images. They have only 2,000 labeled images across 5 defect types. Training a deep CNN from scratch would require millions of images. The team wants to leverage pre-trained models to achieve high accuracy with limited data.
question.question-text: Which transfer learning approach maximizes performance with limited data?

choices.choice: Train a simple CNN from scratch on the 2,000 images
Generate synthetic images to reach millions of samples
Use pre-trained model features without any fine-tuning
Fine-tune a pre-trained ImageNet model, freezing early layers and training later layers and classifier

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: With only 2,000 images, how do you leverage knowledge already learned on millions of other images?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fine-tuning a pre-trained model with layer freezing optimizes for limited data. Pre-trained ImageNet models (ResNet, EfficientNet) have learned general visual features (edges, textures, shapes) transferable to defect detection. Freezing early layers preserves these general features. Training later layers and the classifier adapts the model to defect-specific patterns. This requires far fewer images than training from scratch. Data augmentation further extends the effective dataset. Scratch training overfits on 2,000 images. No fine-tuning may miss domain-specific features. Synthetic generation is complex.

ul.li: Layer freezing: set trainable=False for convolutional base during initial training
Gradual unfreezing: unfreeze layers progressively for fine control
Lower learning rates for fine-tuning prevent destroying pre-trained weights
SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained models with fine-tuning scripts
Augmentation (rotation, flip, brightness) effectively multiplies dataset size

question.title: Batch Inference for Large Datasets
question.scenario: A marketing team needs to score 50 million customer records with a churn prediction model monthly. The scoring job should complete within 4 hours. There's no requirement for real-time predictions. Cost efficiency is important as this is a monthly batch process.
question.question-text: Which inference approach is most appropriate?

choices.choice: Real-time endpoint processing records sequentially
Lambda function invoked for each record
SageMaker Batch Transform with multiple instances for parallel processing
SageMaker Processing job with custom inference script

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Does this workload need responses in real time, or can all records be scored in one run?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Batch Transform is designed for this exact use case. Batch Transform spins up multiple instances, distributes input data automatically, runs inference in parallel, and writes results to S3. For 50M records in 4 hours, configure sufficient instance count for throughput. Infrastructure terminates after job completion - no ongoing costs. Data parallelism across instances handles volume efficiently. Real-time endpoints waste resources when no real-time need exists. Lambda has 15-minute limits and invocation overhead. Processing jobs require custom inference code.

ul.li: Batch Transform auto-splits input files across instances for parallelism
Instance count calculation: total_records / (throughput_per_instance * time_limit)
Max concurrent transforms limit parallel batch jobs organization-wide
Join source data with predictions using input filter and join source settings
GPU instances accelerate batch inference for deep learning models

question.title: A/B Testing ML Models
question.scenario: An online retailer has two recommendation models: the current production model and a new model claiming 10% improvement. They need to validate the new model with real users before full deployment. The test should detect a 10% improvement with 95% confidence within 2 weeks. Business impact must be measured accurately.
question.question-text: Which approach provides statistically valid A/B testing for ML models?

choices.choice: Deploy new model to 50% of users immediately
Compare offline evaluation metrics from test datasets
Run both models on same requests and compare outputs
SageMaker endpoint with production variants and traffic splitting, with statistical significance monitoring

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider controlled experiments with random traffic assignment and proper statistical analysis.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker production variants enable proper A/B testing. Configure endpoint with two variants - assign 90% traffic to production model (control) and 10% to new model (treatment). Random user assignment ensures unbiased comparison. Track business metrics (click-through rate, conversion, revenue) per variant. Calculate sample size for 10% effect detection with 95% confidence. Monitor until statistical significance reached. Offline metrics don't reflect real behavior. 50% immediately risks business impact. Shadow testing doesn't measure actual user response.

ul.li: Sample size calculation: n = 16 * variance / (effect_size^2) for 95% confidence
Variant weights control traffic percentage: VariantWeight parameter
CloudWatch metrics per variant enable comparison dashboards
Sequential testing methods allow early stopping when significance reached
Multi-armed bandit algorithms dynamically shift traffic to better performers

question.title: Data Validation Pipeline
question.scenario: A credit risk model retrains weekly on new application data. Last month, a data pipeline bug caused missing values in key features, leading to degraded model performance. The team needs automated data validation that catches quality issues before training, including schema validation, statistical checks, and anomaly detection.
question.question-text: Which approach implements comprehensive data validation?

choices.choice: SageMaker Processing job with data validation rules, integrated into training pipeline with conditional execution
Manual review of sample data before each training
Train model and evaluate performance to detect issues
Unit tests checking file existence only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider automated validation integrated into ML pipelines with quality gates.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Processing with validation rules in the training pipeline provides systematic data quality checks. Define validation rules: schema checks (column types, names), statistical checks (null rates, distributions, value ranges), and anomaly detection (drift from baseline). Processing jobs execute these checks as a pipeline step. Conditional execution halts training if validation fails, preventing bad models. Results publish to CloudWatch for alerting. Manual review doesn't scale weekly. Training then detecting wastes resources. File existence doesn't validate content.

ul.li: Great Expectations library provides declarative data validation rules
SageMaker Pipelines ConditionStep branches based on validation results
Baseline statistics from training data establish expected distributions
Data profiling reports track quality metrics over time
Integration with Model Registry blocks registration of poorly-trained models

question.title: Neural Architecture Search
question.scenario: A computer vision team is designing a CNN architecture for mobile deployment with strict latency (50ms) and model size (10 MB) constraints. Manual architecture design hasn't achieved the accuracy target. The team wants to automatically search for optimal architectures within the hardware constraints.
question.question-text: Which approach automates architecture discovery with constraints?

choices.choice: Use the largest ResNet variant
Try all published architectures manually
SageMaker Autopilot or AutoGluon with custom objective including latency and size penalties
Randomly generate architectures until one meets constraints

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When manual design can't hit the accuracy target under hardware constraints, what can search the design space for you?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: AutoML tools with custom objectives enable constrained architecture search. AutoGluon (SageMaker integration) supports multi-objective optimization combining accuracy, latency, and model size. The search explores architectures meeting size/latency constraints while maximizing accuracy. Techniques include efficient architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet variants) and neural architecture search algorithms. Custom evaluators measure actual inference latency on target hardware. Manual enumeration is slow. Largest models violate constraints. Random search is inefficient.

ul.li: AutoGluon TabularPredictor supports time_limit and memory constraints
Multi-objective: accuracy - lambda*(latency - target) - mu*(size - limit)
Efficient architectures: MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-Lite designed for mobile
Quantization reduces model size 4x with minimal accuracy impact
SageMaker Neo compiles models optimized for target deployment hardware

question.title: Serverless Inference for Variable Workloads
question.scenario: A sentiment analysis API receives unpredictable traffic - sometimes 100 requests per minute, sometimes 0 for hours. During idle periods, maintaining warm endpoints wastes money. Cold start latency up to 30 seconds is acceptable for this non-critical workload. Model size is 200 MB.
question.question-text: Which inference option minimizes costs for sporadic traffic?

choices.choice: Lambda function with embedded model
Real-time endpoint with minimum 1 instance
Batch Transform triggered on schedule
SageMaker Serverless Inference with configured memory and concurrency

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What deployment model avoids paying for idle compute when traffic is bursty and unpredictable?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Serverless Inference optimizes costs for variable traffic. Serverless endpoints scale to zero when idle - no charges during inactive periods. When requests arrive, containers initialize and serve inference. Memory configuration (up to 6 GB) accommodates the 200 MB model. Max concurrency limits parallel requests. Cold start within 30 seconds is acceptable per requirements. Pay only for inference duration. Real-time endpoints charge continuously. Batch Transform doesn't suit on-demand requests. Lambda has 250 MB deployment limit.

ul.li: Serverless pricing: per-second compute + per-request charge
Memory options: 1024 MB to 6144 MB in 1024 MB increments
Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts for latency-sensitive variants
Model containers remain warm for several minutes after last request
CloudWatch metrics: ModelSetupTime shows cold start duration

question.title: Model Retraining Triggers
question.scenario: A product recommendation model's performance degrades over time as user preferences and catalog change. The team needs to determine when retraining is necessary rather than running on a fixed schedule. Unnecessary retraining wastes compute, while delayed retraining hurts user experience. Performance metrics and data drift should both inform retraining decisions.
question.question-text: Which approach optimizes retraining frequency?

choices.choice: Continuous retraining on every new data point
SageMaker Model Monitor for drift detection combined with business metric monitoring, triggering retraining via EventBridge
Manual decision based on user complaints
Fixed weekly retraining schedule

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Should you retrain on a fixed schedule, or let the data tell you when the model has gone stale?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Model Monitor with business metrics creates intelligent retraining triggers. Model Monitor detects data drift (feature distribution changes) and model quality drift (prediction distribution changes) automatically. CloudWatch metrics track business KPIs (click-through rate, conversion). EventBridge rules trigger retraining pipelines when drift exceeds thresholds OR business metrics decline. This balances computational cost with model freshness. Fixed schedules may retrain unnecessarily or too late. User complaints are lagging indicators. Continuous retraining is expensive.

ul.li: Drift thresholds: statistical tests (KS, Chi-square) with configurable p-value
EventBridge rule: trigger on SageMaker Model Monitor constraint violation event
Combine drift and performance: trigger if drift AND performance decline
Champion/challenger: continuously train challenger models, promote when better
Retraining budget: limit maximum retraining frequency to control costs

question.title: Text Preprocessing for NLP
question.scenario: A customer service team wants to classify support tickets into categories. Tickets contain informal language, typos, special characters, and varying formats. The team needs to preprocess text before training a classification model, handling these variations while preserving the meaning needed for accurate classification.
question.question-text: Which preprocessing pipeline prepares text data appropriately?

choices.choice: Converting all text to ASCII codes
No preprocessing to preserve original text
Only removing extra whitespace
Lowercasing, punctuation removal, tokenization, stop word removal, and optional stemming/lemmatization

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider text normalization steps that reduce noise while preserving semantic content.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Standard NLP preprocessing normalizes text for consistent modeling. Lowercasing treats "Help" and "help" identically. Punctuation removal eliminates non-semantic characters. Tokenization splits text into words/subwords for model input. Stop word removal (optional) eliminates common words like "the", "is". Stemming/lemmatization reduces words to roots ("running" → "run"). This reduces vocabulary size and focuses on meaningful content. No preprocessing increases vocabulary and noise. Whitespace only leaves inconsistencies. ASCII codes lose semantic meaning.

ul.li: Modern transformers (BERT) often prefer minimal preprocessing due to subword tokenization
Domain-specific stop words may include "ticket", "support" in this context
Lemmatization (WordNet) is more accurate than stemming (Porter) but slower
Consider preserving negations ("not", "don't") which flip meaning
SageMaker BlazingText handles basic preprocessing internally

question.title: Ensemble Methods for Improved Accuracy
question.scenario: A fraud detection team has trained multiple models: XGBoost, Random Forest, and Neural Network. Each model has different strengths - XGBoost catches amount-based fraud, Neural Network detects behavioral patterns. Individually, each achieves 92% accuracy. The team wants to combine them for better performance.
question.question-text: Which ensemble approach maximizes combined model performance?

choices.choice: Random selection of which model to use per prediction
Stacking ensemble with meta-learner trained on base model predictions
Using only the best single model
Simple averaging of all model predictions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How can you go beyond simple averaging to learn which model to trust in different situations?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Stacking with a meta-learner optimally combines diverse models. Each base model generates predictions (or probabilities) as features for the meta-learner. The meta-learner (typically logistic regression or XGBoost) learns which model to trust in different situations. This exploits the diversity - XGBoost's amount-based strength complements Neural Network's behavioral patterns. Cross-validation generates out-of-fold predictions to avoid overfitting. Simple averaging doesn't weight model strengths. Single model loses diversity benefit. Random selection adds variance.

ul.li: Stacking uses k-fold CV: train base models on k-1 folds, predict on holdout
Meta-features: probability outputs from each base model, not just predictions
Include original features in meta-learner for richer context
Regularized meta-learner prevents overfitting to base model quirks
AutoGluon implements multi-layer stacking automatically

question.title: Privacy-Preserving ML
question.scenario: Multiple hospitals want to train a disease prediction model on their combined patient data without sharing raw patient records due to HIPAA regulations. Each hospital has valuable data, but no single hospital has enough for a robust model. The solution must enable collaborative learning while protecting patient privacy.
question.question-text: Which approach enables privacy-preserving collaborative ML?

choices.choice: Share encrypted patient records between hospitals
Collect all data in a central location with anonymization
Train separate models at each hospital
Federated learning where models train locally and only gradients are shared

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Can multiple organizations collaborate on a model without any raw data ever crossing institutional boundaries?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Federated learning enables collaborative ML without data sharing. Each hospital trains the model locally on their patient data. Only model updates (gradients) are sent to a central aggregator - no raw patient data leaves the hospital. The aggregator combines gradients from all hospitals to improve the global model, which is then distributed back. This satisfies HIPAA as protected health information stays local. Differential privacy can add noise to gradients for additional protection. Centralized data violates privacy. Separate models lose collective benefit. Encrypted sharing still requires data movement.

ul.li: Federated averaging: average gradients weighted by each participant's dataset size
Secure aggregation encrypts gradients so aggregator can't see individual contributions
Differential privacy adds calibrated noise to prevent membership inference attacks
AWS offers federated learning through partner solutions and custom implementations
Communication efficiency: gradient compression reduces bandwidth requirements

question.title: Handling Missing Data

question.question-text: Which approach handles missing data most appropriately for this scenario?

choices.choice: Delete all rows with any missing values
Fill all missing values with zero
XGBoost's native missing value handling combined with feature-specific imputation for high-missing columns
Fill all missing values with column means

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: XGBoost with selective imputation optimizes missing data handling. XGBoost natively handles missing values - during training, it learns optimal directions for missing value splits. For features with 30% missing, consider domain-specific imputation (sensor reading patterns) or missingness indicators as additional features. Features with only 5% missing can rely on XGBoost's native handling. This preserves information about missingness patterns which may be predictive (sensor failure predicts equipment issues). Deleting rows loses 15%+ of data. Zero or mean imputation loses missingness signal.

ul.li: XGBoost learns split direction for missing values during tree construction
Missingness indicator: binary feature indicating original value was missing
Multiple imputation: generate several imputed datasets, train ensemble
KNN imputation uses similar samples to estimate missing values
MICE (Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations) for complex missing patterns

question.title: Concept Drift Detection
question.scenario: A customer lifetime value model was trained on pre-pandemic data. Post-pandemic, customer behavior changed significantly - spending patterns, channel preferences, and engagement metrics all shifted. The model's predictions are now systematically wrong. The team needs to detect such fundamental changes in the underlying data-generating process.
question.question-text: Which approach detects concept drift effectively?

choices.choice: Retrain on fixed schedule regardless of drift
Only monitor input feature distributions
Check model accuracy on original test set periodically
Monitor prediction performance against delayed ground truth, combined with feature distribution monitoring and domain-specific alerts

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider monitoring approaches that detect changes in the relationship between features and targets.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Concept drift detection requires monitoring the feature-target relationship, not just feature distributions. Even if input distributions remain stable, the relationship to outcomes may change. Monitor prediction performance (accuracy, calibration) against actual outcomes when ground truth becomes available. Track residual distributions over time. Domain-specific alerts catch known disruption patterns (e.g., major events). Feature drift monitoring catches data drift but misses pure concept drift. Original test set doesn't reflect current distribution. Fixed schedules may miss or wastefully respond to drift.

ul.li: Concept drift: P(Y|X) changes while P(X) may stay constant
Virtual drift: P(X) changes without P(Y|X) changing - may not need retraining
Page-Hinkley test detects mean changes in performance metrics over time
ADWIN (Adaptive Windowing) automatically adjusts detection window size
Prediction uncertainty increase often signals concept drift before performance drops

question.title: Feature Selection Methods
question.scenario: A credit scoring model uses 500 features from application data, bureau data, and behavioral data. Many features are correlated, some are noisy, and model training takes 4 hours. The team wants to reduce features to improve training speed, reduce overfitting, and increase model interpretability while maintaining predictive power.
question.question-text: Which feature selection approach balances these requirements?

choices.choice: Combine correlation filtering, recursive feature elimination with XGBoost importance, and domain expert review
Use all 500 features for maximum information
Randomly select 50 features
Keep only features with highest individual correlation to target

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Can one selection technique alone handle correlation, predictive power, and business relevance?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multi-stage feature selection optimizes the feature set systematically. First, correlation filtering removes highly correlated features (keeping most predictive of pair). Then, model-based methods like recursive feature elimination (RFE) with XGBoost importance identify features contributing to predictions. Finally, domain experts validate that selected features make business sense and aren't proxies for protected attributes. This reduces dimensions while preserving predictive signal. All features cause overfitting and slow training. Random selection ignores information content. Individual correlation misses interaction effects.

ul.li: Correlation threshold: typically remove one feature if |r| > 0.9
RFE iteratively removes least important features and refits model
Permutation importance measures feature contribution through shuffling
LASSO regularization provides embedded feature selection during training
Stability selection assesses which features consistently appear across resamples

question.title: Evaluation Metrics Selection
question.scenario: A medical diagnostic model predicts whether patients have a rare disease (1% prevalence). Missing a positive case (false negative) is much more costly than a false alarm (false positive) since early treatment saves lives. The team needs to select appropriate metrics for model evaluation and threshold tuning.
question.question-text: Which metrics are most appropriate for this classification problem?

choices.choice: Accuracy only
ROC AUC only
Recall, Precision-Recall AUC, and F2 score (weighted toward recall)
Specificity (true negative rate)

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When missing a true positive is far more costly than a false alarm, which metric matters most?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Recall-focused metrics align with the asymmetric cost structure. Recall (sensitivity) measures the proportion of actual positives correctly identified - critical when missing cases is costly. Precision-Recall AUC better evaluates imbalanced classes than ROC AUC. F2 score weights recall twice as heavily as precision, matching the cost asymmetry. Threshold tuning on these metrics finds the operating point balancing sensitivity with practical false positive rates. Accuracy is misleading at 1% prevalence (99% accuracy by predicting all negative). ROC AUC can look good while missing most positives. Specificity focuses on negatives.

ul.li: F-beta score: (1 + beta^2) * (precision * recall) / (beta^2 * precision + recall)
Precision-Recall curve shows tradeoff at different classification thresholds
Cost-sensitive learning: weight positive class loss by cost_FN/cost_FP ratio
Calibration curves verify predicted probabilities match actual frequencies
Operating point selection: choose threshold meeting minimum recall requirement

question.question-text: Which service provides end-to-end ML pipeline orchestration?

SageMaker Pipelines with conditional steps, model registry, and EventBridge triggers

ConditionStep branches based on model performance metrics - deploy only if better than baseline. Model Registry stores approved models with metadata and approval workflows. Pipelines are versioned and reproducible - same input produces same output. EventBridge triggers pipelines on S3 data arrival or CloudWatch schedules. Built-in lineage tracks artifacts across pipeline executions. Manual notebooks don't scale. Lambda lacks ML integration. Step Functions require custom ML orchestration.

ul.li: Pipeline steps: Processing, Training, Tuning, Transform, RegisterModel, Condition, Fail
Condition step: JsonGet evaluates metrics from evaluation step output
Model Registry: model groups, versions, approval status, deployment history
Pipeline parameters enable dynamic values (data path, hyperparameters) at runtime

question.title: Data Augmentation for Limited Training Data
question.scenario: A wildlife conservation team has only 500 images of an endangered species for an identification model. Collecting more images is impractical. question.question-text: Which data augmentation strategy maximizes effective training data?

choices.choice: Generate completely synthetic images using GAN
Only horizontal flipping
Duplicate images without modification
Geometric transforms (rotation, flip, crop), color augmentation, and mixup/cutout with careful validation monitoring

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: With only 500 real images, how can you synthetically expand the training set without distorting species features?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Comprehensive augmentation significantly expands effective training data. Geometric transforms (rotation, horizontal flip, random crop, scale) simulate different viewpoints and distances. Color augmentation (brightness, contrast, saturation) handles lighting variation. Mixup blends images for regularization. Cutout masks random patches, improving robustness. Important: validate that augmentations preserve species-identifying features. Monitor validation performance to detect harmful augmentation (e.g., vertical flip may create unrealistic poses). Single augmentation provides limited benefit. GANs require large datasets to train well. Exact duplicates don't add information.

ul.li: Albumentations library provides fast, diverse image augmentations
AutoAugment learns optimal augmentation policies from data
Mixup: blend images and labels, e.g., 0.7*img1 + 0.3*img2, label=[0.7, 0.3]

Test-time augmentation: average predictions across augmented versions for inference

question.title: Regularization Techniques
question.scenario: A neural network for customer churn prediction achieves 95% accuracy on training data but only 75% on validation data - clear overfitting. The model has 10 million parameters trained on 100,000 samples. The team needs to reduce overfitting while maintaining the model's capacity to learn complex patterns.
question.question-text: Which regularization techniques address this overfitting?

choices.choice: Increase model size
Train for more epochs
Remove validation set
Dropout layers, L2 weight regularization, early stopping based on validation loss, and batch normalization

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider techniques that constrain model complexity and prevent memorization of training data.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multiple regularization techniques together combat severe overfitting. Dropout randomly deactivates neurons during training, preventing co-adaptation and acting like ensemble averaging. L2 regularization penalizes large weights, encouraging simpler solutions. Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving, preventing over-optimization on training data. Batch normalization stabilizes training and provides mild regularization. The 20% accuracy gap requires strong regularization. More epochs worsen overfitting. Larger models have more capacity to overfit. Validation set is essential for detecting overfitting.

ul.li: Dropout rate: typically 0.2-0.5, higher for larger layers
L2 regularization adds lambda * sum(weights^2) to loss function
Early stopping patience: number of epochs to wait before stopping
Data augmentation also acts as regularization by expanding effective training set
DropConnect: randomly drops weights rather than activations

question.title: Model Compression for Deployment
question.scenario: A deep learning model achieves excellent accuracy but is too large (2 GB) and slow (500ms inference) for mobile deployment. The target device has limited memory (500 MB available) and requires inference under 100ms. Model accuracy can degrade slightly (up to 2%) if deployment constraints are met.
question.question-text: Which techniques reduce model size and latency for deployment?

choices.choice: Only optimize the inference code
Use a larger server for inference
Increase batch size during inference
Quantization (FP32 to INT8), pruning of low-magnitude weights, and knowledge distillation to smaller architecture

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider model compression techniques that reduce size and computation while preserving accuracy.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Model compression techniques address all deployment constraints. Quantization converts 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers, reducing model size by 4x and accelerating inference on hardware with INT8 support. Pruning removes weights with small magnitudes (near-zero contribution), reducing both size and computation. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic the large teacher model's outputs, often achieving similar accuracy with 10x fewer parameters. Combined, these can achieve 10-20x compression. Larger servers don't address mobile deployment. Batch size doesn't reduce per-inference latency. Code optimization alone can't achieve 4x size reduction.

ul.li: Post-training quantization: simple, no retraining, small accuracy loss
Quantization-aware training: fine-tune with quantization simulation for better accuracy
Structured pruning removes entire channels/filters for hardware speedup
SageMaker Neo compiles and optimizes models for target hardware
ONNX Runtime provides optimized inference across platforms

question.title: Model Security and Adversarial Robustness
question.scenario: A content moderation model classifies images as safe or unsafe. Adversaries attempt to bypass the model by adding imperceptible perturbations to unsafe images, causing misclassification. The team needs to detect adversarial inputs and improve model robustness against such attacks.
question.question-text: Which approaches improve model robustness against adversarial attacks?

choices.choice: Add CAPTCHA before classification
Encrypt the model weights
Use a larger model
Adversarial training with generated adversarial examples, input validation, and ensemble with diverse models

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider defense techniques that make models resilient to adversarial perturbations.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Defense-in-depth improves adversarial robustness. Adversarial training augments training data with adversarial examples (generated using FGSM, PGD attacks), teaching the model to correctly classify perturbed inputs. Input validation detects anomalous inputs - adversarial images often have unusual pixel distributions or high-frequency patterns. Ensembles of models with different architectures are harder to fool simultaneously - attacks optimized for one model often fail on others. Model encryption protects IP, not against adversarial inputs. Model size doesn't address adversarial robustness. CAPTCHA verifies humans, not content.

ul.li: FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method): single-step attack using gradient direction
PGD (Projected Gradient Descent): iterative attack, stronger than FGSM
Input preprocessing: JPEG compression, spatial smoothing remove perturbations
Certified defenses provide provable robustness within perturbation bounds
Adversarial detection: train classifier to distinguish clean vs adversarial inputs

question.title: Embedding Generation for Similarity Search
question.scenario: An e-commerce company wants to find similar products based on images and descriptions. The solution should combine both visual and text similarity for comprehensive matching.
question.question-text: Which approach enables efficient multi-modal similarity search?

choices.choice: Generate image embeddings with CNN and text embeddings with transformer, combine into multi-modal vectors, and index in OpenSearch k-NN
Compare raw images pixel by pixel
Full-text search on product descriptions only
Store all products in memory for exhaustive comparison

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How do you make 10 million items searchable by visual and textual similarity in under 50ms?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multi-modal embeddings with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search provides efficient similarity. Pre-trained CNN (ResNet, EfficientNet) generates image embeddings capturing visual features. Transformer models (BERT, sentence-transformers) generate text embeddings from descriptions. Concatenate or fuse embeddings into unified multi-modal vectors. OpenSearch k-NN plugin indexes vectors using HNSW algorithm for sub-50ms approximate nearest neighbor search on 10M vectors. This combines visual and semantic similarity. Pixel comparison is computationally infeasible. Text-only misses visual similarity. Exhaustive comparison doesn't scale.

ul.li: CLIP model generates aligned image and text embeddings in shared space
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) provides logarithmic search complexity
Embedding dimension reduction (PCA) reduces storage and search time
Hybrid search: combine k-NN similarity with keyword filtering
OpenSearch k-NN supports cosine similarity, L2 distance, and inner product

question.title: Time Series Forecasting Architecture

question.question-text: Which forecasting approach handles this multi-series prediction with uncertainty?

Train 1,000 separate ARIMA models
Random walk forecast (tomorrow = today)
Amazon Forecast or SageMaker DeepAR with related time series for external factors and quantile forecasts

hint.content: Can a single model learn shared patterns across 1,000 locations while still giving confidence intervals?

Amazon Forecast automates model selection and hyperparameter optimization. Separate ARIMA models don't share learning across series. Single regression loses center-specific patterns. Random walk doesn't capture trends.

ul.li: DeepAR uses autoregressive RNN generating probabilistic forecasts
Related time series: categorical (center type) and dynamic (promotions, weather)
Amazon Forecast AutoML tests multiple algorithms (DeepAR, Prophet, ARIMA)
Quantile forecasts: P10 for optimistic, P50 for expected, P90 for conservative planning
Cold start handling: DeepAR forecasts new series using learned global patterns

question.title: Model Inference Optimization
question.scenario: A computer vision model serves real-time image classification with strict 100ms latency requirement at P99. Currently, inference takes 80ms average but P99 reaches 200ms due to variable preprocessing time and occasional cold starts. The model runs on GPU instances with auto-scaling.
question.question-text: Which optimizations reduce P99 latency below 100ms?

choices.choice: Add more auto-scaling capacity
Asynchronous preprocessing, warm instance pool, request batching, and TensorRT optimization
Increase instance size
Cache all possible predictions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider optimizations targeting both cold starts and variable processing latency.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multiple optimizations together reduce P99 latency. Asynchronous preprocessing overlaps CPU image processing with GPU inference for previous request. Warm instance pool (minimum instances > 0) eliminates cold starts that cause latency spikes. Request batching amortizes fixed overhead across multiple images when traffic allows. TensorRT optimizes the model graph for GPU, reducing inference time by 2-5x. Together, these address both the variable preprocessing (async) and cold start (warm pool) contributors to P99 spikes. Larger instances don't address cold starts. More auto-scaling capacity doesn't reduce latency. Prediction caching doesn't work for unique images.

ul.li: TensorRT: layer fusion, precision calibration (FP16/INT8), kernel auto-tuning
Dynamic batching: accumulate requests up to timeout, process together
Provisioned concurrency in Serverless Inference eliminates cold starts
GPU memory pre-allocation avoids allocation latency during inference
CUDA streams enable overlapping data transfer and computation

question.title: Synthetic Data Generation
question.scenario: A financial institution wants to share customer data with a third-party ML vendor for model development, but privacy regulations prevent sharing real customer data. They need to generate synthetic data that preserves statistical properties needed for ML while ensuring no real customer can be identified in the synthetic dataset.
question.question-text: Which approach generates privacy-safe synthetic data for ML?

choices.choice: Replace names with fake names only
Train a generative model (VAE or GAN) on real data with differential privacy guarantees
Randomly shuffle columns independently
Sample from uniform distributions for each feature

hint.content: How can you produce realistic-looking data for a vendor while mathematically bounding re-identification risk?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Generative models with differential privacy produce useful synthetic data safely. VAEs (Variational Autoencoders) or GANs learn the joint distribution of features, preserving correlations essential for ML. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise during training, mathematically bounding information leakage about any individual. Generated samples are statistically similar but not copies of real data. Membership inference tests verify synthetic data doesn't reveal original records. Column shuffling destroys feature correlations. Name replacement leaves other PII. Uniform distributions lose statistical properties.

ul.li: Differential privacy epsilon parameter controls privacy-utility tradeoff
CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) designed for tabular data generation
Privacy metrics: membership inference attack success rate should be ~50% (random)
Utility metrics: compare ML model performance on real vs synthetic data
