question.title: Foundation Model Fine-Tuning
question.scenario: A legal services company wants to use a large language model for contract analysis. General-purpose LLMs lack legal domain knowledge and make errors on jurisdiction-specific terms. The company has 10,000 annotated legal documents. They want to adapt a foundation model to their domain without full model retraining, which would be prohibitively expensive.
question.question-text: Which approach efficiently adapts a foundation model to the legal domain?

choices.choice: Train a legal LLM from scratch
Prompt engineering only without any fine-tuning
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA or adapter layers) on Amazon Bedrock or SageMaker JumpStart
Fine-tune all model parameters on the legal dataset

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Full retraining of a billion-parameter model is too expensive. Is there a way to teach it a new domain cheaply?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts foundation models cost-effectively. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adds small trainable matrices to frozen model layers, learning domain-specific patterns with 0.1% of original parameters. Amazon Bedrock supports fine-tuning foundation models with custom datasets. SageMaker JumpStart provides fine-tuning for open-source models. 10,000 documents are sufficient for PEFT but not from-scratch training. This approach preserves general capabilities while adding legal knowledge. From-scratch requires billions of tokens and massive compute. Prompt engineering alone can't encode domain terminology. Full fine-tuning is expensive and risks catastrophic forgetting.

ul.li: LoRA adds low-rank decomposition matrices: W + BA where B, A are small
Adapter layers insert small trainable modules between transformer layers
Bedrock custom model training supports fine-tuning Claude, Titan, and others
Instruction tuning format: input context, instruction, expected output
Evaluation: compare fine-tuned vs base model on held-out legal test set

question.title: Feature Store Real-Time Serving
question.scenario: A ride-sharing app needs to make pricing decisions in real-time based on current demand features (recent trip counts, driver availability, surge indicators). Features must be computed from streaming data and available for inference within 1 second of underlying events. The same features are used for model training on historical data.
question.question-text: Which architecture supports real-time feature serving with training consistency?

choices.choice: Store raw events in DynamoDB and compute at inference time
Kinesis for streaming, Lambda computing features, SageMaker Feature Store online store for serving and offline store for training
Daily batch feature computation stored in S3
Compute features in the inference request itself

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Features must be fresh within 1 second for inference yet also available historically for training. What architecture serves both?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Streaming feature pipeline with Feature Store provides real-time serving with consistency. Kinesis ingests streaming events (trips, driver status). Lambda processes streams computing features (10-minute trip counts, driver counts). Features push to Feature Store online store for millisecond retrieval during inference. The same features automatically sync to offline store (S3) for training, ensuring training-serving consistency. Feature definitions are centralized, preventing skew. Request-time computation adds latency and duplicates logic. Daily batch has unacceptable lag. Raw event querying doesn't scale.

ul.li: Feature Store online: single-digit millisecond reads via GetRecord API
Streaming ingestion: PutRecord API with automatic offline sync
Feature freshness SLA: configure acceptable staleness for each feature group
Point-in-time correctness: offline queries retrieve features as of event timestamp
Feature pipelines should be idempotent for replay and recovery

question.title: Model Fairness Evaluation
question.scenario: A hiring platform uses an ML model to screen resumes. Regulators require demonstrating the model doesn't discriminate based on protected attributes (gender, race, age). The company needs to measure fairness metrics, identify potential bias, and document compliance. Some protected attributes aren't explicit features but may be correlated with other features.
question.question-text: Which approach provides comprehensive fairness evaluation?

choices.choice: Check if protected attributes are used as features
Manual review of rejected candidates
Compare average predictions across groups
SageMaker Clarify for pre-training data bias, post-training model bias, and SHAP-based feature attribution across groups

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Removing protected attributes from features isn't enough. Why might bias still creep in through correlated features?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Clarify provides multi-faceted fairness evaluation. Pre-training bias analysis detects imbalances in training data (class imbalance across groups). Post-training model bias measures outcome disparities using multiple metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, disparate impact). SHAP analysis shows which features drive predictions differently across groups, catching proxy discrimination (e.g., zip code correlating with race). Clarify generates compliance-ready reports documenting bias assessment. Checking explicit features misses proxy discrimination. Simple average comparison misses nuanced disparities. Manual review doesn't scale and lacks metrics.

ul.li: Demographic parity: P(Y=1|A=0) ≈ P(Y=1|A=1) for protected attribute A
Equalized odds: equal TPR and FPR across groups
Disparate impact ratio: should be > 0.8 (four-fifths rule)
Proxy features: Clarify identifies features correlated with protected attributes
Model cards document fairness evaluation for regulatory compliance

question.title: Data Splitting Strategies
question.scenario: A data scientist is preparing data for a customer churn model. The dataset spans 2 years with 500,000 customers. Customer behavior changes seasonally, and the model will make predictions for future months. The team needs to split data into training, validation, and test sets appropriately to get reliable performance estimates.
question.question-text: Which data splitting strategy provides reliable performance estimates?

choices.choice: Use all data for training, evaluate on training set
Time-based split: train on earlier months, validate on middle period, test on most recent months
Stratified split by churn label only
Random 80/10/10 split across all records

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider temporal ordering when models will predict future outcomes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Time-based splitting mimics real-world deployment for forecasting problems. Train on historical data (e.g., months 1-18), validate hyperparameters on middle period (months 19-21), test on most recent data (months 22-24). This prevents data leakage from future information and tests model performance on truly unseen future data. Seasonal patterns in validation/test reflect deployment reality. Random splits leak future information (model sees 2024 patterns during training then predicts 2023). Stratified split doesn't respect temporal order. Training evaluation gives optimistic, unreliable estimates.

ul.li: Walk-forward validation: expanding window trains on all prior data at each step
Embargo period: gap between train and test prevents label leakage
Purging: remove samples within window of test samples for time series
Grouped time split: keep all records for a customer in same split
Seasonal holdout: ensure test set includes all seasonal patterns

question.title: Anomaly Detection Approaches
question.scenario: A manufacturing system needs to detect equipment anomalies from sensor readings. Normal operation data is abundant, but failure examples are rare and don't cover all possible failure modes. New types of failures should be detected even if never seen before. The model must work in real-time on streaming sensor data.
question.question-text: Which anomaly detection approach handles unseen failure modes?

choices.choice: Rule-based thresholds on individual sensors
Binary classifier trained on normal vs failure examples
Unsupervised anomaly detection (Isolation Forest or autoencoder) trained on normal data only
Time series forecasting predicting exact sensor values

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: If failures are rare and come in forms you've never seen, can a classifier trained on failure examples catch them?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Unsupervised anomaly detection learns normal behavior and flags deviations. Isolation Forest identifies anomalies as points requiring few splits to isolate - normal points are in dense regions. Autoencoders learn to reconstruct normal data; high reconstruction error indicates anomaly. These methods detect any deviation from normal, including unseen failure modes. Training requires only abundant normal data. SageMaker Random Cut Forest provides managed anomaly detection. Binary classifiers only detect seen failure types. Fixed thresholds miss complex multi-sensor patterns. Exact prediction is unnecessary for anomaly detection.

ul.li: Isolation Forest: anomaly score based on average path length in random trees
Autoencoder: compress to latent space and reconstruct, error = anomaly score
Random Cut Forest: streaming algorithm updates model with new data points
Contamination parameter: expected proportion of anomalies in training data
Multi-variate analysis detects anomalies in sensor combinations, not individual sensors

question.title: Multi-Region ML Deployment
question.scenario: A global streaming service needs to deploy recommendation models across 5 AWS regions to serve users with low latency. Models should be consistent across regions. When models update, all regions should receive the new version within 1 hour. Regional failures shouldn't affect other regions. Model artifacts are 5 GB each.
question.question-text: Which architecture enables resilient multi-region ML deployment?

choices.choice: CloudFront caching inference responses
Single region serving all global traffic
Manual model copying to each region
S3 Cross-Region Replication for model artifacts, CodePipeline with parallel regional deployments, and Route 53 latency-based routing

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How do you keep 5 GB model artifacts in sync across 5 regions within an hour without manual steps?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multi-region architecture provides global low-latency with resilience. S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies model artifacts to regional buckets within minutes. CodePipeline deploys to all 5 regions in parallel when models update, achieving 1-hour rollout. Each region has independent SageMaker endpoints - regional failures are isolated. Route 53 latency-based routing directs users to nearest healthy region. Health checks fail over traffic if a region has issues. Single region adds latency for distant users. Manual copying doesn't meet 1-hour requirement. CloudFront can't cache dynamic recommendations.

ul.li: S3 replication time control (RTC) guarantees 15-minute replication SLA
CodePipeline cross-region actions deploy to multiple regions from single pipeline
Route 53 health checks detect endpoint failures for automatic failover
Global Accelerator provides static IPs with automatic regional failover
Endpoint naming convention includes region for deployment automation

question.title: Automated Model Remediation
question.scenario: A production fraud detection model occasionally experiences performance degradation when fraud patterns change. Currently, the team manually investigates and retrains when issues are detected. They want to automate the response: when model performance drops below threshold, trigger investigation, and if confirmed, automatically initiate retraining with recent data.
question.question-text: Which architecture automates model remediation?

choices.choice: Daily scheduled retraining regardless of performance
CloudWatch alarms on Model Monitor metrics triggering Step Functions workflow for validation and conditional pipeline execution
Manual monitoring of CloudWatch dashboards
Ignore drift until users complain

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Manual investigation is slow. What if the system could detect degradation, verify it, and kick off retraining on its own?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Event-driven remediation automates the response to model degradation. Model Monitor publishes metrics to CloudWatch when quality violations occur. CloudWatch alarms trigger when performance drops below thresholds. Step Functions workflow receives the alarm: first validates the issue (queries additional metrics, checks data quality), then conditionally triggers SageMaker Pipeline for retraining if confirmed. Approval gates can require human confirmation for production deployment. This responds quickly to real issues without unnecessary retraining. Fixed schedules may miss rapid changes or waste compute. Manual monitoring delays response. Waiting for complaints harms users.

ul.li: Step Functions error handling: retry failed steps, catch exceptions, fallback paths
Validation step queries ground truth labels to confirm performance drop
SageMaker Pipeline parameters pass recent data dates for retraining
SNS notifications keep team informed of automated actions
Rollback capability: keep previous model for quick recovery if retraining fails

question.title: Multimodal Data Fusion
question.scenario: A real estate valuation model needs to predict property prices using structured data (square footage, bedrooms, location), property images (interior, exterior), and text descriptions (agent listing descriptions). Each modality provides different information. The team needs to effectively combine these diverse data types into a unified model.
question.question-text: Which architecture fuses multimodal data for unified predictions?

choices.choice: Use only the most predictive single modality
Convert all data to tabular format
Separate encoders for each modality (tabular, CNN for images, transformer for text) with late fusion concatenating embeddings before final prediction layers
Average predictions from three separate models

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Images, text, and tabular data each need different processing. At what stage should their signals merge?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Late fusion with modality-specific encoders effectively combines multimodal data. Each encoder is optimized for its data type: tabular network for structured features, CNN (ResNet) for images extracting visual features (quality, style, views), transformer for text understanding listing language. Encoders produce fixed-size embeddings capturing modality-specific information. Concatenated embeddings feed into final prediction layers learning cross-modal interactions. This leverages each modality's strengths. Converting images/text to tabular loses rich information. Single modality ignores valuable signals. Separate model averaging misses cross-modal relationships.

ul.li: Early fusion: concatenate raw features before any processing
Late fusion: combine high-level representations from separate encoders
Cross-attention fusion: modalities attend to each other for richer interaction
Pretrained encoders: use frozen ImageNet CNN, BERT for text
Modality dropout: randomly drop modalities during training for robustness

question.title: Experiment Tracking and Reproducibility
question.scenario: A data science team of 10 people runs hundreds of experiments weekly testing different features, algorithms, and hyperparameters. They struggle to track which configurations produced the best results, reproduce successful experiments, and compare results across team members. Notebooks with embedded results are scattered across laptops.
question.question-text: Which approach provides systematic experiment management?

choices.choice: SageMaker Experiments with automatic metric logging, artifact tracking, and visual comparison tools
Spreadsheet logging experiment results manually
Git commits for each experiment
Email results to team members

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When 10 people run hundreds of experiments weekly, how do you avoid losing track of what worked and why?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Experiments provides centralized experiment management. Experiments organizes related runs into logical groups. Automatic tracking captures hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts (model files, plots) without manual logging. Trial comparison visualizes metrics across experiments for selecting best configurations. Artifact storage enables reproducing any experiment by accessing exact inputs and outputs. Team members access shared experiment history. Lineage connects experiments to deployed models. Spreadsheets require manual entry and lack artifact tracking. Git commits don't capture metrics and results well. Email doesn't enable systematic comparison.

ul.li: Trial components: atomic units capturing inputs, outputs, parameters, metrics
Experiment analytics: query and filter experiments by parameter ranges
Automatic tracking in training jobs: metrics logged to Experiments automatically
Artifact versioning: track exact data and model versions for each trial
Integration with MLflow for teams already using MLflow tracking
